claim: The hippocampus is believed to encode episodic memory by binding information about the content of experience within a spatiotemporal framework encoding the location and temporal context of that experience.
source: The hippocampus is believed to encode episodic memory by binding information about the content of experience within a spatiotemporal framework encoding the location and temporal context of that experience.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific theory about hippocampal function in episodic memory.

claim: Previous work implies a distinction between positional inputs to the hippocampus from upstream brain regions that provide information about an animal's location and nonpositional inputs which provide information about the content of experience, both sensory and navigational.
source: Previous work implies a distinction between positional inputs to the hippocampus from upstream brain regions that provide information about an animal's location and nonpositional inputs which provide information about the content of experience, both sensory and navigational.
evidence: This claim references prior research findings about hippocampal input organization.

claim: Rats navigated freely on a novel maze consisting of linear segments arranged in a rectilinear, city-block configuration.
source: Rats navigated freely on a novel maze consisting of linear segments arranged in a rectilinear, city-block configuration, which combined elements of open-field foraging and linear-track tasks.
evidence: This describes the experimental apparatus and behavioral paradigm used in the study.

claim: Place fields were directionally tuned on the maze, even though the animal's behavior was not constrained to extended, one-dimensional (1D) trajectories.
source: Unlike typical results in open-field foraging, place fields were directionally tuned on the maze, even though the animal's behavior was not constrained to extended, one-dimensional (1D) trajectories.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data showing directional tuning in a 2D environment.

claim: Repeating fields from the same cell tended to have the same directional preference when the fields were aligned along a linear corridor of the maze.
source: Repeating fields from the same cell tended to have the same directional preference when the fields were aligned along a linear corridor of the maze, but they showed uncorrelated directional preferences when they were unaligned across different corridors.
evidence: This is a key experimental finding about the relationship between field location and directional tuning.

claim: Repeating fields showed uncorrelated directional preferences when they were unaligned across different corridors.
source: Repeating fields from the same cell tended to have the same directional preference when the fields were aligned along a linear corridor of the maze, but they showed uncorrelated directional preferences when they were unaligned across different corridors.
evidence: This is a key experimental finding demonstrating dissociation of nonpositional inputs across repeating fields.

claim: Individual fields displayed complex time dynamics which resulted in the population activity changing gradually over the course of minutes.
source: Lastly, individual fields displayed complex time dynamics which resulted in the population activity changing gradually over the course of minutes.
evidence: This describes temporal dynamics observed in the neural recordings.

claim: Temporal dynamics were evident across repeating fields of the same cell.
source: These temporal dynamics were evident across repeating fields of the same cell.
evidence: This describes how temporal dynamics manifested in repeating place fields.

claim: The positional inputs that drive a cell to fire in similar locations across the maze can be behaviorally and temporally dissociated from the nonpositional inputs that alter the firing rates of the cell within its place fields.
source: These results demonstrate that the positional inputs that drive a cell to fire in similar locations across the maze can be behaviorally and temporally dissociated from the nonpositional inputs that alter the firing rates of the cell within its place fields, offering a potential mechanism to increase the flexibility of the system to encode episodic variables within a spatiotemporal framework provided by place cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The dissociation between positional and nonpositional inputs offers a potential mechanism to increase the flexibility of the system to encode episodic variables within a spatiotemporal framework provided by place cells.
source: These results demonstrate that the positional inputs that drive a cell to fire in similar locations across the maze can be behaviorally and temporally dissociated from the nonpositional inputs that alter the firing rates of the cell within its place fields, offering a potential mechanism to increase the flexibility of the system to encode episodic variables within a spatiotemporal framework provided by place cells.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The hippocampus is critically dependent on allocentric space representation within a distributed, interconnected network of regions.
source: In the mammalian brain, allocentric space is represented within a distributed, interconnected network of regions that specialize in different aspects of spatial experience (O'Keefe, 1976; Taube, 1998; Hafting et al., 2005; Alexander and Nitz, 2017; Nitz, 2012; Sharp, 1999). This navigation system is critically dependent on the hippocampus, whose pyramidal cells have spatial firing fields that are distributed throughout the environment to provide a continuous representation of position (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; O'Keefe, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Hippocampal pyramidal cells have spatial firing fields that are distributed throughout the environment to provide a continuous representation of position.
source: This navigation system is critically dependent on the hippocampus, whose pyramidal cells have spatial firing fields that are distributed throughout the environment to provide a continuous representation of position (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; O'Keefe, 1976).
evidence: This is a well-established finding in hippocampal research, supported by citations.

claim: The CA1 region receives spatially tuned inputs from regions such as CA3 (other place cells) and the entorhinal cortex (grid cells, spatial non-grid cells, landmark-vector cells).
source: The CA1 region receives spatially tuned inputs from regions such as CA3 (other place cells) and the entorhinal cortex (grid cells, spatial non-grid cells, landmark-vector cells) that influence where a CA1 place field is located.
evidence: This describes the anatomical and functional connectivity of CA1.

claim: Place cells form the basis of a cognitive map within which the items and events of an organism's experience are located and interrelated in support of episodic memory.
source: These place cells are thought to form the basis of a cognitive map within which the 'items and events of an organism's experience are located and interrelated' (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978, p. 1) in support of episodic memory.
evidence: This is the cognitive map theory, supported by citation to O'Keefe and Nadel.

claim: CA1 neurons respond to odors.
source: CA1 neurons respond to odors (Wiener et al., 1989; Wood et al., 1999; Wiebe and Stäubli, 1999; Komorowski et al., 2009; Allen et al., 2016), tones (Moita et al., 2003; Aronov et al., 2017), textures (Itskov et al., 2011), and tastants (Herzog et al., 2019; Herzog et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: CA1 neurons respond to tones.
source: CA1 neurons respond to odors (Wiener et al., 1989; Wood et al., 1999; Wiebe and Stäubli, 1999; Komorowski et al., 2009; Allen et al., 2016), tones (Moita et al., 2003; Aronov et al., 2017), textures (Itskov et al., 2011), and tastants (Herzog et al., 2019; Herzog et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CA1 neurons respond to textures.
source: CA1 neurons respond to odors (Wiener et al., 1989; Wood et al., 1999; Wiebe and Stäubli, 1999; Komorowski et al., 2009; Allen et al., 2016), tones (Moita et al., 2003; Aronov et al., 2017), textures (Itskov et al., 2011), and tastants (Herzog et al., 2019; Herzog et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: CA1 neurons respond to tastants.
source: CA1 neurons respond to odors (Wiener et al., 1989; Wood et al., 1999; Wiebe and Stäubli, 1999; Komorowski et al., 2009; Allen et al., 2016), tones (Moita et al., 2003; Aronov et al., 2017), textures (Itskov et al., 2011), and tastants (Herzog et al., 2019; Herzog et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CA1 neurons can be influenced by internal variables such as subjective frames of reference.
source: and they can be influenced by internal variables such as subjective frames of reference (Gothard et al., 1996; Jackson and Redish, 2007; Fenton et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hippocampal neurons respond to travel direction.
source: For example, neurons have been recorded that respond to travel direction (McNaughton et al., 1983; Wiener et al., 1989; Markus et al., 1995), prospective and retrospective turns or positions (Wood et al., 2000; Ferbinteanu and Shapiro, 2003; Smith and Mizumori, 2006; Ji and Wilson, 2008), entire trajectories (Grieves et al., 2016a), and speed (McNaughton et al., 1983; Czurkó et al., 1999; Maurer et al., 2012; Huxter et al., 2003; Wiener et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Hippocampal neurons respond to prospective and retrospective turns or positions.
source: For example, neurons have been recorded that respond to travel direction (McNaughton et al., 1983; Wiener et al., 1989; Markus et al., 1995), prospective and retrospective turns or positions (Wood et al., 2000; Ferbinteanu and Shapiro, 2003; Smith and Mizumori, 2006; Ji and Wilson, 2008), entire trajectories (Grieves et al., 2016a), and speed (McNaughton et al., 1983; Czurkó et al., 1999; Maurer et al., 2012; Huxter et al., 2003; Wiener et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hippocampal neurons respond to entire trajectories.
source: For example, neurons have been recorded that respond to travel direction (McNaughton et al., 1983; Wiener et al., 1989; Markus et al., 1995), prospective and retrospective turns or positions (Wood et al., 2000; Ferbinteanu and Shapiro, 2003; Smith and Mizumori, 2006; Ji and Wilson, 2008), entire trajectories (Grieves et al., 2016a), and speed (McNaughton et al., 1983; Czurkó et al., 1999; Maurer et al., 2012; Huxter et al., 2003; Wiener et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Hippocampal neurons respond to speed.
source: For example, neurons have been recorded that respond to travel direction (McNaughton et al., 1983; Wiener et al., 1989; Markus et al., 1995), prospective and retrospective turns or positions (Wood et al., 2000; Ferbinteanu and Shapiro, 2003; Smith and Mizumori, 2006; Ji and Wilson, 2008), entire trajectories (Grieves et al., 2016a), and speed (McNaughton et al., 1983; Czurkó et al., 1999; Maurer et al., 2012; Huxter et al., 2003; Wiener et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In many studies, the firing rates of neurons changed while the locations of the firing field stayed stable, a phenomenon termed 'rate remapping'.
source: In many of the examples above, and related studies, the firing rates of the neurons changed while the locations of the firing field stayed stable (Leutgeb et al., 2005; Herzog et al., 2019; Moita et al., 2003; Wood et al., 2000). It should be noted that in at least one study some place fields shifted their center of mass in response to combinatorial cue changes, although this study also reported in-field firing rate changes as well (Anderson and Jeffery, 2003). These findings, termed 'rate remapping', inspired the hypothesis (Leutgeb et al., 2005) of a functional dissociation between where the neuron fires and the quantitative rate of firing within the field (see also Shapiro et al., 1997; Manns and Eichenbaum, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Rate remapping inspired the hypothesis of a functional dissociation between where the neuron fires and the quantitative rate of firing within the field.
source: These findings, termed 'rate remapping', inspired the hypothesis (Leutgeb et al., 2005) of a functional dissociation between where the neuron fires and the quantitative rate of firing within the field (see also Shapiro et al., 1997; Manns and Eichenbaum, 2009).
evidence: This is a theoretical hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: CA1 neurons have multiple fields under different circumstances, for instance in large environments or environments with repeated structural elements.
source: CA1 neurons have multiple fields under different circumstances, for instance in large environments (Rich et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2020; Park et al., 2011; Harland et al., 2021) or environments with repeated structural elements.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Place field repetition is defined as a neuron with multiple spatial firing fields at instances of a repeated structural element or behavioral motif.
source: The latter, termed 'place field repetition' (Spiers et al., 2015; Grieves et al., 2017), is defined as a neuron with multiple spatial firing fields at instances of a repeated structural element or behavioral motif, such as a repeated trajectory, in an environment.
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations.

claim: Many different types of repeating track structure can elicit place field repetition in CA1.
source: For CA1, many different types of repeating track structure can elicit place field repetition, e.g., multiple boxes arranged in a row (Skaggs and McNaughton, 1998; Spiers et al., 2015; Grieves et al., 2016b), a spiral track (Cowen and Nitz, 2014), a spiral staircase (Hayman et al., 2011), or an M-maze or hairpin maze (Frank et al., 2000; Derdikman et al., 2009; Singer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Repetition has been observed outside of the hippocampus, in the entorhinal cortex, subiculum, and retrosplenial cortex.
source: Repetition has also been observed outside of the hippocampus, in the entorhinal cortex (Frank et al., 2000), subiculum (Stewart et al., 2014), and retrosplenial cortex (Alexander and Nitz, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Repeating fields of the same neuron do not always display the same nonpositional rate modulation.
source: Here, we show that repeating fields of the same neuron do not always display the same nonpositional rate modulation, demonstrating that nonpositional cues are dissociable from the positional inputs onto place cells in a given environment.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: On average, 14.7 cells per session (5–35 cells) were recorded that met the inclusion criteria for detailed analysis.
source: On average, 14.7 cells per session (5–35 cells) were recorded that met the inclusion criteria for detailed analysis (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the sample size of the experimental data.

claim: Repeating fields were equally likely to be in vertical or horizontal alleys.
source: Repeating fields were equally likely to be in vertical or horizontal alleys (167 horizontal versus 146 vertical fields, chi-square goodness of fit, compared to a null distribution of equal numbers of horizontal and vertical fields, χ2(1)=1.41, p=0.235).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: Each repeating cell had up to seven fields.
source: Each repeating cell had up to seven fields, suggesting that repetition was spatially modulated at the level of the apparatus, as no cell had fields at each alley (mean number of repeating fields = 3.55 ± 1.46 fields; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the experimental data, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: No cell had fields at each alley, suggesting that repetition was spatially modulated at the level of the apparatus.
source: Each repeating cell had up to seven fields, suggesting that repetition was spatially modulated at the level of the apparatus, as no cell had fields at each alley (mean number of repeating fields = 3.55 ± 1.46 fields; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Place field repetition was not driven by the presence of poorly isolated units.
source: Place field repetition was not driven by the presence of poorly isolated units that combined multiple fields into one 'cell', as there was no significant difference in cell quality between repeating and non-repeating neurons included in the analysis (Mann-Whitney U=3214, p=0.1).
evidence: This is a control analysis to rule out a technical artifact.

claim: The mean orientation alignment score (OAS) of multi-fielded cells was significantly greater than expected by chance (mean = 0.71, 95th percentile shuffle = 0.64).
source: The mean OAS of multi-fielded cells was significantly greater than expected by chance (mean = 0.71, 95th percentile shuffle = 0.64, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data, with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Multiple fields of a neuron tend to share a positional input that instructs them where to fire.
source: This result demonstrates that multiple fields of a neuron tend to share a positional input that instructs them where to fire.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the OAS finding.

claim: A significant subset of fields was directionally tuned (93/310 fields passed a Mann-Whitney test per field; binomial test, p=3.6 × 10–45).
source: Across the population, a significant subset of fields was directionally tuned (Figure 3B; 93/310 fields passed a Mann-Whitney test per field; binomial test, p=3.6 × 10–45).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Directional fields had a difference in normalized firing that was two-thirds more than their mean firing.
source: The mean difference in normalized directional firing was 1.67±2.20 for fields that passed the Mann-Whitney test and 0.69±0.72 for those that did not. In other words, directional fields had a difference in normalized firing that was two-thirds more than their mean firing.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the directional tuning strength.

claim: A GLM analysis identified a subset of fields with a significant effect of current direction (103/297 fields, binomial test p=4.53 × 10–57).
source: This analysis identified a subset of fields with a significant effect of current direction (Figure 3C, 103/297 fields, binomial test p=4.53 × 10–57; note that the total number of fields, i.e., the denominator, is different here than for the Mann-Whitney test due to the sampling requirements of the two tests [see Materials and methods]).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis, with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The random forest classifier successfully decoded direction from the population activity in 10/20 orientation-filtered datasets (binomial test p=1.13 × 10–8).
source: The random forest classifier successfully decoded direction from the population activity in 10/20 orientation-filtered datasets (binomial test p=1.13 × 10–8, FWER-corrected alpha = 0.05, Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the decoding analysis, with reference to Figure 3E.

claim: The distributions of average normalized firing rate differences in each direction were not statistically different between repeating and non-repeating neurons.
source: However, the distributions of average normalized firing rate differences in each direction (analyzed as in Figure 3B) were not statistically different between repeating and non-repeating neurons, with a mean difference of 0.88 normalized Hz for the repeating fields and 1.21 normalized Hz for the non-repeating fields (Mann-Whitney U=11,883, p=0.49; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between repeating and non-repeating fields, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The proportions of directional fields were not different between repeating and non-repeating groups (69/172 repeating fields versus 51/125 non-repeating fields, Pearson's chi-square χ2(1)=0.001, p=0.97).
source: Further, the proportions of directional fields were not different between the groups (69/172 repeating fields versus 51/125 non-repeating fields, Pearson's chi-square χ2(1)=0.001, p=0.97).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between repeating and non-repeating fields.

claim: Repeating fields were equally likely to be directionally tuned as non-repeating fields.
source: These data indicate that repeating fields were equally likely to be directionally tuned as non-repeating fields and those that were directional in each group had similar tuning strength.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical comparisons.

claim: Position could be reliably decoded from the population activity (median performance above 95th percentile of shuffled data in 10/10 datasets, binomial test p=9.76 × 10–14).
source: Position could be reliably decoded from the population activity (median performance above 95th percentile of shuffled data in 10/10 datasets, binomial test p=9.76 × 10–14; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the position decoding analysis, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Both repeating and non-repeating neurons were similarly informative about position (average difference = 0.06 ± 0.21, t-test compared to 0, t(8) = 0.923, p=0.38).
source: The difference in decoding performance between subpopulations of repeating and non-repeating neurons (with the larger group downsampled) shows that both groups of neurons were similarly informative about position (average difference = 0.06 ± 0.21, t-test compared to 0, t(8) = 0.923, p=0.38; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of decoding performance, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: Field pairs on the same corridor had a significant positive correlation in their directional tuning (OLS r2=0.237, p=0.00012).
source: Field pairs from the same corridor had a significant positive correlation in their directional tuning (OLS r2=0.237, p=0.00012, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the corridor analysis, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Pairs on different corridors were not correlated with one another (OLS r2=0.017, p=0.125).
source: However, pairs on different corridors were not correlated with one another (OLS r2=0.017, p=0.125, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the corridor analysis, with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: The correlations between same corridor and different corridor field pairs were significantly different from one another (Z=2.49, p=0.0063).
source: These correlations were significantly different from one another (Z=2.49, p=0.0063, one-sided independent sample Fisher's Z-transformation test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between the two corridor conditions.

claim: The weak positive correlation in the total population of pairs is explained by a stronger correlation among the same corridor field pairs alone.
source: These data suggest that the weak positive correlation in the total population of pairs is explained by a stronger correlation among the same corridor field pairs alone.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the corridor analysis results.

claim: A GLM approach identified a significant number of fields that exhibited significant time dynamics (83/296 oriented fields; binomial test, p=2.07 × 10–38).
source: Across all cells, a GLM approach identified a significant number of fields that exhibited significant time dynamics (83/296 oriented fields; binomial test, p=2.07 × 10–38; average increase in fit 0.26±0.38; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the temporal dynamics analysis, with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Repeating and non-repeating fields were equally likely to exhibit temporal dynamics (66/171 repeating fields, 39/125 non-repeating fields, Pearson's chi-square χ2(1)=0.53, p=0.42).
source: Repeating and non-repeating fields were equally likely to exhibit temporal dynamics, demonstrating a similar lack of difference seen in directional tuning (66/171 repeating fields, 39/125 non-repeating fields, Pearson's chi-square χ2(1)=0.53, p=0.42).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between repeating and non-repeating fields.

claim: Fields from the same repeating neuron were not more likely to be correlated or anticorrelated with one another in their time dynamics (mean correlation = 0.049 ± 0.26).
source: This distribution was centered at zero, suggesting fields were not more likely to be correlated or anticorrelated with one another (mean correlation = 0.049 ± 0.26).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the temporal correlation analysis.

claim: More distant time windows were less correlated (average slope per dataset –0.06±0.022, two-sided t-test compared to 0, t(9) = 7.88, p=2.49 × 10–5).
source: More distant windows were less correlated (average slope per dataset –0.06±0.022, two-sided t-test compared to 0, t(9) = 7.88, p=2.49 × 10–5; Figure 6D), consistent with prior work (Manns et al., 2007; Mankin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the population vector correlation analysis, with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: The decoding performance was high near the training window and decayed outside of it, yielding a positive slope (mean Spearman correlation = 0.44 ± 0.49) before the training window and a negative slope (mean Spearman correlation = –0.45 ± 0.43) after the training window.
source: This analysis revealed that the decoding performance was high near the training window and decayed outside of it, yielding a positive slope (mean Spearman correlation = 0.44 ± 0.49, one-sided t-test (greater), t=7.59, p=5.11 × 10–11) to the performance in the window before the training window and a negative slope (mean Spearman correlation = –0.45 ± 0.43, one-sided t-test (less), t=10.0, p=1.53 × 10–16) to the performance after the training window (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the sliding window decoding analysis, with reference to Figure 6F.

claim: The presence of directional firing on a maze that had properties of both open-field foraging and directed navigation tasks suggested that the low degrees of freedom for path choices resulted in the system distinguishing between the paths.
source: First, the presence of directional firing on a maze that had properties of both open-field foraging and directed navigation tasks suggested that the low degrees of freedom for path choices resulted in the system distinguishing between the paths, possibly because they differed from one another in limited ways constrained by the geometry of the apparatus rather than continuously, as they would on an open platform.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the directional firing results.

claim: Comparing directional tuning across repeating fields revealed a distinction between positional inputs and nonpositional inputs.
source: Second, comparing directional tuning across repeating fields revealed a distinction between positional inputs (i.e. inputs that tell a place cell where to fire) and nonpositional inputs (i.e. inputs, including spatial inputs, that tell a place cell how strongly to fire in its place field).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the repeating field analysis.

claim: The map maintained a stable spatial signal but exhibited gradual temporal dynamics, with repeating fields showing temporally dissociable changes similar to their dissociation in directionality.
source: Last, in spite of the spatial ambiguity introduced by multi-fieldedness and temporal dynamics, the map maintained a stable spatial signal but exhibited gradual temporal dynamics, with repeating fields showing temporally dissociable changes similar to their dissociation in directionality.
evidence: This is a summary of the temporal dynamics findings.

claim: Place fields are more directional when animals perform directed, stereotyped trajectories on unidimensional tracks compared to 2D foraging in an open field.
source: Place fields are more directional when animals perform directed, stereotyped trajectories on unidimensional tracks (McNaughton et al., 1983; Markus et al., 1995; Liberti et al., 2022) compared to 2D foraging in an open field (Muller et al., 1994; Markus et al., 1995; but see Rubin et al., 2014; Acharya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of prior research findings, supported by citations.

claim: The combination of place field repetition and directionality has been interpreted as evidence for trajectory encoding, or 'path equivalence'.
source: This combination of place field repetition and directionality has been interpreted as evidence for trajectory encoding, or 'path equivalence', in which spatially selective neurons in the hippocampus or entorhinal cortex fire in similar locations along a trajectory that is repeated at different locations in an environment.
evidence: This is a summary of a theoretical interpretation from prior research.

claim: Trajectory coding by repeating fields is likely to be more complex than previously characterized.
source: The data presented here suggest that trajectory encoding by repeating fields is likely to be more complex than previously characterized (Frank et al., 2000; Singer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current study's findings in relation to prior work.

claim: Many repeating fields were uncorrelated in their responses to direction, showing that directional preference per se was not the driving force underlying repetition under the conditions of the present study.
source: In the present work, many repeating fields were uncorrelated in their responses to direction (at least when the repeating fields were on different corridors), showing that directional preference per se was not the driving force underlying repetition under the conditions of the present study.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the directional tuning analysis of repeating fields.

claim: A subset of repeating fields showed strong correlations in their firing rates across the different types of complex trajectories through the fields.
source: Although the lack of shared directional preference in many neurons suggested that these neurons were not encoding trajectories in a simple manner, we nonetheless observed that the repeating fields of many cells showed strong correlations in their firing rates across the different types of complex trajectories through the fields (i.e. previous, current, and next alleys) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a finding from the trajectory analysis, with reference to Figure 5G.

claim: Many repeating fields in different corridors were anticorrelated in their trajectory responses.
source: However, many repeating fields in different corridors were anticorrelated in their trajectory responses.
evidence: This is a finding from the trajectory analysis.

claim: Place field repetition may result from multiple mechanisms that give rise to similar phenomena: a subset of repeating fields may encode trajectory while another subset encodes a different dimension, such as local border geometry.
source: Thus, place field repetition may result from multiple mechanisms that give rise to similar phenomena: a subset of repeating fields may encode trajectory while another subset encodes a different dimension, such as local border geometry.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the trajectory analysis results.

claim: The potential contribution of local border geometry to place field repetition is supported by multiple studies and was specifically proposed as a mechanism in one modeling study.
source: The potential contribution of local border geometry to place field repetition is supported by multiple studies and was specifically proposed as a mechanism in one modeling study (Grieves et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a summary of prior research, supported by citation.

claim: Cells were disproportionately likely to have fields with borders on the same sides of the field, i.e., to be aligned along an axis of the maze (vertical or horizontal).
source: Cells in the present work were disproportionately likely to have fields with borders on the same sides of the field, i.e., to be aligned along an axis of the maze (vertical or horizontal) (this is similar to axis-tuned cells reported by Olson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, with comparison to prior work.

claim: It is plausible that repetition may be caused by stronger border-related input to these neurons.
source: Thus, it is plausible that repetition may be caused by stronger border-related input to these neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on known inputs to CA1.

claim: Place field repetition offers a unique opportunity to explore how inputs are functionally organized in CA1.
source: Place field repetition offers a unique opportunity to explore how inputs are functionally organized in CA1.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the experimental approach.

claim: The present data provide evidence that this process is assisted by individual field 'addressability', wherein different nonpositional inputs affect a neuron's response differently at different fields.
source: The present data provide evidence that this process is assisted by individual field 'addressability', wherein different nonpositional inputs (i.e. experiential inputs) affect a neuron's response differently at different fields.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Both the positional signal and the nonpositional signal could be retrieved from a multiplexed coding scheme.
source: Our population decoding analyses demonstrated that both the positional signal and the nonpositional signal could be retrieved from such a multiplexed coding scheme.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoding analyses.

claim: Repeating place fields provided a within-cell control to demonstrate that positional inputs and nonpositional inputs are organized differently in CA1.
source: Repeating place fields provided a within-cell control to demonstrate that positional inputs (e.g. functional influences that tell a place field where to fire) and nonpositional inputs (i.e. functional influences that tell the neuron how strongly to fire in its field) are organized differently in CA1.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental approach and its implications.

claim: Different repeating fields can show different directional preferences, meaning fields do not inherit their nonpositional tuning as a global property of the cell.
source: The present data utilize repeating fields to suggest that different repeating fields can show different directional preferences. In other words, fields do not inherit their nonpositional tuning as a global property of the cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the directional tuning analysis of repeating fields.

claim: The present data suggest that the nonpositional inputs are always flexible, as expected if they encode the episodic content of an experience on a stable spatial framework.
source: Regardless of whether the positional inputs are rigid or flexible across environments, the present data suggest that the nonpositional inputs are always flexible, as expected if they encode the episodic content of an experience on a stable spatial framework.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The difference in corridor was correlated with behavioral biases in how animals sampled fields.
source: The difference in corridor was also correlated with behavioral biases in how animals sampled fields.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis.

claim: The present data demonstrate a constant, gradual drift in the population activity pattern as the animal forages without a task.
source: The present data demonstrate a constant, gradual drift in the population activity pattern as the animal forages without a task.

claim: Although the map maintains spatial informativeness at each point in time, the activity of the neurons comprising the map exhibits strong temporal non-stationarities.
source: This affects the stability of the map over time; although the map maintains spatial informativeness at each point in time, the activity of the neurons comprising the map exhibits strong temporal non-stationarities.

claim: The time dynamics within individual repeating fields were heterogeneous and uncorrelated.
source: The time dynamics within individual repeating fields were heterogeneous and uncorrelated.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal dynamics analysis.

claim: The fluctuations over time were not always synchronized across repeating fields, providing evidence for another nonpositional signal that is not conserved across fields.
source: These time dynamics do not necessarily correspond to the encoding of time per se, and further experiments would be needed to make that claim. For example, unknown variables that change over time may be altering the firing of these cells. However, the relevance of time dynamics for the present study is that the fluctuations over time were not always synchronized across repeating fields. This provides evidence for another nonpositional signal, time, or some temporally varying signal, that is not conserved across fields.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal dynamics findings.

claim: For most repeating cells the positional input was stable in that it provided a consistent instruction for where to fire as the field drifted.
source: However, it is also important to note that for most repeating cells the positional input was stable in that it provided a consistent instruction for where to fire as the field drifted; fields tended to drift between analogous locations.
evidence: This is an observation about the stability of positional coding during temporal drift.

claim: CA1 activity patterns are constantly drifting even in the absence of a task but in a way that preserves the spatial informativeness of the map.
source: Therefore, the present data show that CA1 activity patterns are constantly drifting even in the absence of a task (as demonstrated previously in LEC; Tsao et al., 2018) but in a way that preserves the spatial informativeness of the map.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal dynamics analysis, with comparison to prior work.

claim: Place cells do not receive a global gain signal that affects all fields equally.

claim: The behavioral sampling of an environment may affect how the CA1 place map represents it.
